principles.text: Focus on entries offering asymmetric risk/reward: limited downside represented by a tight stop, entered where the trend is changing, so price should start trending in your favor immediately rather than chopping sideways.
Use EMA stacking and slope (e.g. 9/21/50/150 EMA order and direction) to objectively classify a stock as trending vs. sideways/choppy before deciding whether to trade it.
After a strong gap-up move, wait for a pullback into the 9 or 21 EMA before entering long rather than chasing the initial breakout.
Avoid chasing (FOMO) a setup that already looks good but has run too far without you in it; wait for the next proper opportunity instead.
Cover shorts into weakness/extension and lock in profits; the entry price of your next short in the same name is generally going to be higher (worse) than where you covered.
The more extended the market/sector becomes to the downside, the more you should trim/cover shorts, since a snapback bounce after an extended move tends to be fast and strong.
In choppier, more volatile conditions, trail a winning trend-following position with a wider EMA (e.g. 21 EMA) rather than a tighter one (9 EMA) to avoid getting shaken out prematurely.
You don't need a strong technical reason to take profits into weakness on a short - it's always fine to cover some or all when it feels right, because there will always be another opportunity.
Use small risk per trade, especially early in a trading career, to keep drawdowns manageable while you're still gaining experience from losses.
Deep drawdowns commonly trace back to overtrading, taking poor entries, ignoring your own stop-loss, and oversizing positions - not just bad luck.

Use the price action that follows a stop-out as feedback: if the stopped-out position reverses and gaps back above key levels the next day, the broader thesis/market condition may not be as bad as it looked and re-entry can be considered; if it instead breaks down further, that confirms the weakness.
Specialize in the setup type/side (e.g. shorts only, or a specific pattern) that matches your demonstrated edge rather than trying to trade every opportunity in every direction.

Journal your trades after a drawdown and look for patterns in the mistakes, including non-trading factors (personal life, mood, sleep) that may have contributed, so you can recognize the same warning signs in the future.
Review your good/winning trades, not just losses, to identify what made them work and to rebuild confidence during a drawdown.
Copying another trader's system can work as a starting point, but it isn't sustainable long-term - you eventually need to tweak and adapt the rules to fit your own personality.
Taking a loss/getting stopped out isn't inherently bad - it can be useful information that prompts a shift in bias (e.g. from long to short focus).
Gauge overall market health by watching how a broad list of individual stocks is behaving, rather than relying on a single indicator (like a follow-through day) to call a market bottom or top.
After an ambiguous, volatile session with a sharp bounce, stay open-minded to either direction (continuation lower or a real reversal) rather than committing hard to one bias.

The specific pattern (e.g. tight-range consolidation breakout) matters less than whether it satisfies the underlying requirement of asymmetric risk/reward; keep trading a setup only as long as that requirement still holds, even if the pattern occurs less frequently in the current market.
